title: Split Context Provider Simulator
concept: Separating State from Dispatch in React Context
problemStatement: Implement `createSplitContext(initialState)` that creates distinct state and dispatch channels, allowing dispatch functions to maintain stable identity forever.
interviewTrap: Components that only need `dispatch` (like buttons) should NEVER re-render when state changes. Splitting context achieves this.

testCases.name: Dispatch function has strictly stable reference identity
testCases.testFn: const ctx = createSplitContext({ count: 0 }); return ctx.getDispatch() === ctx.getDispatch();

testCases.name: Dispatching updates state listeners
testCases.testFn: const ctx = createSplitContext({ count: 0 }); let updated = 0; ctx.subscribeState(s => { updated = s.count; }); ctx.getDispatch()({ count: 1 }); return updated;

testCases.name: Supports functional action updates
testCases.testFn: const ctx = createSplitContext({ count: 10 }); ctx.getDispatch()(prev => ({ count: prev.count + 5 })); return ctx.getState().count;

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: When a Context Provider's `value` prop changes identity, EVERY component that calls `useContext(MyContext)` MUST re-render, bypassing any `React.memo` or `shouldComponentUpdate` checks. Splitting into separate `StateContext` and `DispatchContext` prevents dispatch consumers from re-rendering on state changes.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Why is splitting Context into StateContext and DispatchContext a recommended performance pattern?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Because in React Context, ANY update to the context value forces ALL consuming components (`useContext`) to re-render. If state and dispatch are bundled in one object (`{ state, dispatch }`), every state update creates a new object reference, forcing components that only need `dispatch` (like action buttons) to re-render unnecessarily! Splitting into `StateContext` and `DispatchContext` ensures dispatch consumers never re-render because `dispatch` is referentially stable.

realWorldUseCases.description: Splitting user authentication data from login/logout action dispatchers.
realWorldUseCases.codeSnippet: const UserStateCtx = createContext(); const UserDispatchCtx = createContext();

howToExplain.opening: Splitting Context into independent State and Dispatch contexts decouples state consumers from action triggers, eliminating unnecessary re-renders.
keyPoints: Context re-renders all consumers when provider value reference changes.
Dispatch functions from useReducer are referentially stable.
Components needing only dispatch never re-render when state changes.
Simple, native pattern for scalable state management without third-party libraries.
howToExplain.closingImpression: Splitting context provides Redux-like performance using 100% native React primitives.
analogies: Separating a TV screen from the remote control: the TV screen updates continuously, but the remote control in your hand never needs to change.

commonMistakes.mistake: Passing an inline object literal to Context.Provider value: `<Ctx.Provider value={{ state, dispatch }}>`.
commonMistakes.why: Creates a brand new object on every provider render, forcing all consumers to re-render even if state did not change.
commonMistakes.correct: Wrap the value object in useMemo.

followUpDeepDive.question: How does React propagate Context updates down the Fiber tree?
followUpDeepDive.answer: When a context value changes, React runs `propagateContextChange` in `ReactFiberNewContext.js`, scanning down the fiber tree and setting lanes on all matching consumer fibers, bypassing `shouldComponentUpdate` and `React.memo` bailouts.
